The red-rumped agouti Dasyprocta leporina, a medium-sized caviomorph rodent inhabiting Neotropical forests, exhibits a reproductive schedule finely tuned to the warm, stable thermal conditions of its equatorial range. Under a constant ambient temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], which approximates the core body temperature at which metabolic and developmental processes are optimized in this species, females are capable of an impressive reproductive output. Field and captive records indicate that litters typically contain 1 to 3 pups [N_R_i = 1 to 3 pups], a litter size characteristic of a precocial mammal that invests heavily in each individual offspring from the moment of parturition. Furthermore, under these same thermal conditions, the inter-birth interval is remarkably short: females can produce 1 to 4 litters per year [F_R_i = 1 to 4 litters per year], a rate that places D. leporina among the more fecund members of the Dasyproctidae. This high reproductive frequency is ecologically significant, compensating for naturally elevated juvenile mortality from predation by ocelots, boas, and raptors across the forest floor. The combination of relatively large litters and rapid sequential breeding ensures population persistence despite heavy predation pressure on young, dispersing individuals.

Neonatal agoutis are notably precocial, entering the world fully furred and with open eyes, a condition reflected in their substantial mass at birth. Recordings from captive breeding colonies show that newborns weigh approximately 213 grams [Wwb = approximately 213 grams], a value that represents a considerable maternal investment during the approximately 112-day gestation (approximately 112 days) [tg = approximately 112 days] at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. The young are mobile within hours of birth and begin sampling solid food remarkably early, yet the period of nutritional dependence on the mother is extensive. At the thermal set point of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], the weaning process is completed by 140 days after birth [tx = 140 days after birth], marking the transition from milk-dependent suckling to full herbivorous foraging. This protracted weaning period, uncommon among rodents of comparable body size, may be adaptive in the context of learning the complex spatial distribution of seasonally fruiting trees and cached seeds, skills that directly determine post-weaning survival. Observations in Trinidad and the Guianas indicate that the mother gradually reduces nursing frequency during the final month, coinciding with the juvenile's increasing ability to crack hard palm nuts independently.

Growth in female agoutis follows a trajectory that culminates in an asymptotic adult body mass reflecting the species' robust build. The ultimate wet weight attained by mature females is 3265 grams [Wwi = 3265 grams], a mass that enables effective seed dispersal through scatterhoarding behavior and provides a substantial buffer against periods of resource scarcity during the dry season. Puberty, however, precedes the attainment of full adult size by a considerable interval, an ontogenetic pattern that allows early commencement of reproductive activity while somatic growth continues. Specifically, when individuals are maintained at 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], the time since birth at which females achieve sexual maturity is approximately 193 days [tp = approximately 193 days]. This early onset of gonadal activity, well before the complete ossification of long bones, is a life-history trait associated with high adult mortality risk and the opportunistic exploitation of ephemeral fruit masts that characterize the agouti's rainforest habitat. It also explains how a female can theoretically conceive her first litter during the same calendar year as her own birth.

Longevity and the duration of gestation are two further life-history parameters that shape the demographic profile of Dasyprocta leporina. At the regulated temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], which standardizes metabolic rate comparisons, the maximum recorded lifespan for this species reaches 17.8 years [am = 17.8 years], a figure that is notably elevated relative to similarly sized myomorph rodents and is more consistent with the slow life histories observed in hystricognath rodents. This extended lifespan, documented in protected captive environments, is coupled with a gestation period of 112 days [tg = 112 days], although field reports from French Guiana and Suriname document a natural range of 104 to 120 days depending on maternal condition and local resource availability at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. The relatively long gestation, among the longest for a rodent of this body mass, yields highly developed neonates and contributes to the low annual adult mortality observed once individuals have survived the vulnerable juvenile stage. This combination of traits—slow embryonic development, extended postpartum care, and exceptional longevity—places the red-rumped agouti as a prime example of the conservative life-history strategy prevalent across the Caviomorpha.

The full life-cycle integration of these traits becomes most apparent when considering the energetic and ecological constraints operating on a scatter-hoarding frugivore. Captive colonies maintained under a strict thermal regime of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] not only sustain rapid reproductive turnover but also illustrate the tight coupling between thermal physiology and developmental timing. Under these conditions, females reach sexual maturity at 193 days after birth [tp = 193 days after birth], which, together with weaning completed by 140 days after birth [tx = 140 days after birth], creates a compressed intergenerational window rarely exceeded in the wild at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. The production of litters with 1 to 3 pups [N_R_i = 1 to 3 pups] and the capacity for 1 to 4 reproductive events per year [F_R_i = 1 to 4 reproductive events per year] underscore a demographic resilience that buffers populations against the high stochastic variability of tropical mast seeding. Meanwhile, the extended lifespan approaching 18 years [am = approaching 18 years] provides numerous breeding opportunities, offsetting years with poor fruiting at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This suite of interrelated life-history parameters—from neonatal mass to senescence—reflects a finely tuned adaptation to the dispersed, unpredictable, and highly competitive resource landscape of the Neotropical forest understory.
